title: The Definition of Alaṅkāra
summary: Defines the alaṅkāra: a pattern of a few notes carried in rhythm through the whole ascent and descent. Its qualities are repetition, reversal, skipping and wandering, fitting a tāla, and following the long and short syllables of words; tables give examples and practice alaṅkāras of four to sixteen beats.

blocks.text: Definition of alaṅkāra

blocks.verse:
यदाऽरोहेऽवरोहे च विशिष्ट क्रमयोजना।
उच्चारो लययोगेन सैवालंकार उच्यते।१०३।
blocks.text: When, in ascent and descent, a particular arrangement of order [among the notes] is made, and it is sounded joined with laya (tempo), that alone is called alaṅkāra (patterned exercise).

That is, when a particular order is arranged among the notes, and ascent and so on are performed with it based on laya (tempo), it is called alaṅkāra (patterned exercise). But bear in mind that an order formed in two or three notes should be carried through the whole ascent and descent. For example, 'Sa Re Ga' and 'Sa Ga Re': both these note groups are made of only three notes, but if the order of the first is 1, 2, 3, then the order of the second is 1, 3, 2. If we carry the first of these orders through 'Re Ga Ma' instead of 'Sa Re Ga', and then through the other notes, the following alaṅkāra will be formed - Sa Re Ga, Re Ga Ma, Ga Ma Pa, Ma Pa Dha, Pa Dha Ni, Dha Ni Ṡa | Ṡa Ni Dha, Ni Dha Pa, Dha Pa Ma, Pa Ma Ga, Ma Ga Re, Ga Re Sa. And by carrying the second order through the other notes - Sa Ga Re, Re Ma Ga, Ga Pa Ma, Ma Dha Pa, Pa Ni Dha, Dha Ṡa Ni | Ṡa Dha Ni, Ni Pa Dha, Dha Ma Pa, Pa Ga Ma, Ma Re Ga, Ga Sa Re - this alaṅkāra will arise.
In alaṅkāras, besides the particular order, there are other subtle elements too.

blocks.verse:
लय ताल समावेशः शब्दानुकरणं तथा।
स्वर शक्ति विकाशश्चे त्येतेऽलंकारजा गुणाः।१०४।
blocks.text: The inclusion of laya (tempo) and tāla (metric cycle), the imitation of words (śabdānukaraṇa), and the development of the power of the notes (svara-śakti): these are the qualities born of alaṅkāra.

As soon as alaṅkāra (patterned exercise) is discussed, three questions arise in the mind: (1) In how many notes is this alaṅkāra arranged? (2) Of how many mātrās (beats) is this order? (3) What is its special feature with regard to cāl (movement)? It is these very questions that are being answered.

The inclusion of laya (tempo) and tāla (metric cycle) in any alaṅkāra, the imitation of words, and the development of the svara-śaktis (powers of the notes) as befits an alaṅkāra, are given below; they resemble the actions described earlier.

blocks.verse:
आवृत्तिस्तु स्वरैके स्वयाद् वैपरीत्यं स्वरद्वये।
स्वरत्रये भवेल्लंघः संचारस्तु चतुष्टये।१०५।
blocks.text: Āvṛtti (repetition) is in one note; vaiparītya (reversal) in two notes; in three notes there is laṅgha (leaping); and sañcāra (movement) in four.

Āvṛtti (repetition) means repeating a note again and again. But if a group of two or three notes is repeated, understand it as dvayāvṛtti (two-note repetition) and trayāvṛtti (three-note repetition) respectively.

blocks.text: This is a simple quality, which is ordinarily possible in anything from one note to many notes. But repetition of more than three is impractical. A somewhat more precious quality lies in two notes: vaiparītya (reversal), that is, being turned over, and being smaller and larger. This quality is impossible in one note, just as, if someone has only one son, it is impossible to decide whether he is the younger or the elder. More precious still is the quality that lives in three notes, or in more than three notes: laṅghita (leaping), that is, leaving out some note in between and going on to a note further ahead. For example, 'Sa Ga'.

Better still is the quality that lives in four notes: (sañcāra) wandering. All the qualities above are possible in many alaṅkāras (patterned exercises); even so, in a given alaṅkāra one quality is found to predominate. For example -

blocks.text: In the same way, on the basis of just three notes, alaṅkāras (patterned exercises) can be made from Dādarā up to Tīntāl, that is, from six mātrās (beats) to 16 mātrās. Making orders of notes according to the short and long syllables in words is called śabdānukaraṇa (imitation of words). If someone spoke a word (paṅkaja), we should understand it as paṃ - ka ja, because uttering paṃ takes more time than 'ka' and 'ja'. Following it, [the notes] will be Sa - Re Ga. Now more examples are presented.

blocks.text: Thoughtful sādhakas (practitioners) make many alaṅkāras (patterned exercises) by mixing, on the basis of these qualities. Here some practical alaṅkāras are presented as examples. The various svara-śaktis (powers of the notes) contained in them, readers will themselves recognize in the form of seeds, and will use them. These alaṅkāras are built in two notes up to four notes. Their length ranges from four mātrās (beats) to 16 mātrās.
Note

It is hoped that learners will carry these alaṅkāras (patterned exercises) through, beginning from every note, will extend their ascending order into a full ascent and descent, and will practise them. Then, if possible, they will also try to make other similar alaṅkāras on the basis of the elements contained in them.

blocks.verse:
नरा नार्यश्च देवाश्च सर्वेऽलंकार भूषिताः।
अलंकारैर्हि लोकाश्च स्वराः काव्याश्च शोभिताः।१०६।
blocks.text: Men, women and gods are all adorned with alaṅkāras (ornaments); by alaṅkāras indeed the worlds, the notes and poems are made beautiful.

That is, the real meaning of alaṅkāra is a means of decoration, that is, an ornament. From Prakṛti (nature) to Puruṣa, all are its takers. In this world men, women, gods, demons, poetry and music: all these honour alaṅkāra.

In the world of musical notes, indeed, nothing works without alaṅkāra. The three states of alaṅkāra are scientific. (1) When the sādhaka (practitioner) arranges certain fixed notes in a particular order and then keeps carrying that order regularly through the following notes, he begins to sense the truth of that order; this state is called sādhyāvasthā (the state of striving). (2) When the sādhaka, absorbed in its unbroken japa (repetition), begins to experience concentration and peace in the mind, this is called the siddhāvasthā (state of attainment) of that alaṅkāra. And when the sādhaka uses it effortlessly in some song or the like, then, in the form of a mirkī (quick turn of notes), it delights people and touches the heart. This third state is called rasapradā (giving rasa). It would be apt if we take these three states as examples of satyam, śivam and sundaram (the true, the good and the beautiful). This is the meaning of the following śloka.

blocks.verse:
तिस्रोऽवस्थाश्च तेषां स्युः साध्या सिद्धा रसप्रदा।
आद्ये विस्तारतानेषु गीतेषु च रसप्रदा।१०६।
blocks.text: They have three states: sādhyā (to be attained), siddhā (attained) and rasapradā (giving rasa). The first [two belong] to vistāra (elaboration) and tānas, and the rasapradā to songs.

If alaṅkāras (patterned exercises) are composed in three notes by the rule of mathematics, using only ekāvṛtti (one-note repetition) with the help of laṅghana (skipping), the following 36 alaṅkāras can be composed.
SaReGaGa SaSaReGa SaReReGa SaGaReGa SaReSaGa - from Sa to Ga --- 5+
SaGaReRe SaSaGaRe SaGaGaRe SaReGaRe SaGaSaRe - from Sa to Re --- 5+
SaReGaSa SaGaReSa  - from Sa to Sa -- 2 = 12
In the same way, beginning from Re and from Ga, there will be 12*3=36 in all.
